utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-02-54-R77.5-T, the case against Ms. Florence Hartmann.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have appearance for today, starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. My name is Bruce MacFarlane. I appear on behalf of the Prosecution, and with me today and throughout the proceedings is Lori Ann Wanlin to my right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. MacFarlane. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, good morning. My name is Karim Khan, and together with Guenal Mettraux and our legal assistant, Samrina Mohamad, we represent Ms. Florence Hartmann.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Khan. May we call the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Kandic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Given the fact the break has been too long, I'll ask you to please make the declaration once again. May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Ms. Kandic, I have a couple of areas that I'd like to speak to you about and ask you questions on. But before we get into anything of a substantive nature: In some of the materials that have been filed in these proceedings by counsel for the accused with reference to your proposed evidence, you were referred to, in particular in the pre-trial brief, as a militant human rights activist, and my question is whether or not you agree with that characterization. And if you do, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm really reluctant to start objecting at this stage, but could Mr. MacFarlane refer to the exact passage or reference he's giving. I have no recollection of us referring to a militant, Your Honour, but if we're incorrect, we'd be grateful for the indication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. MacFarlane, will you give the citation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: It's in the pre-trial brief which was filed on the 15th of January. I won't, at this point, be able to provide the page number, but we'll be able to do that later on this morning, if there's any issue as to that. But the witness could simply make note of the question, and we can return to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: During your evidence, Ms. Kandic, on the last occasion, you made reference to the fact that there was quite a number of press reports and public debate concerning the minutes, notes, and decisions, and I'd like to ask you a series of questions which I'm hoping will be a bit more precise in terms of timing and what was being discussed. But that's the general area I'd like as you about is the press reports and the public debate. Can you be a bit more precise as to what was being discussed and being debated during that period of time before the book came out?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I happen to have with me a specific press report, an article, showing that even those who were members of the legal team of Serbia spoke publicly about the transcripts of the Supreme Defence Council. This is a report by the B92 Radio --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are witnesses allowed to come in with papers into court to read from in this Tribunal, unless they're expert witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: If it refreshes the memory of the witness, I would have no concerns about that, but I'm not sure that it would be appropriate simply to read on and on. That would be my view and my submission. This is not my witness. I'm in cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I know that. I'm just surprised that, in fact, you are silent to the fact that she does have a paper with her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: My expectation was that that was going to be used for the purposes of refreshing her memory. But if it goes further than that, then certainly I would have concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have anything to say about that, Mr. Mettraux?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Not in particular, Your Honour. But about the previous thing, we'd like to apologise to our colleague. We've reached -- we've identified the paragraph, and it says Ms. Kandic is a high-profile militant for human rights. So we apologise, Your Honour. It is indeed used this word in this summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah. I'm sure Mr. MacFarlane will return to that question. Okay, you may proceed, Mr. MacFarlane, if you have no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Ms. Kandic, could you tell us more about what was being debated, the types of press reports that were going out, without necessarily reading a press report. But I'd like to get a sense from you of what was being debated and the nature of the press reports that were coming out during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is very important that I read one sentence. I don't need this paper as a reminder. I know this very well, but I think it is very important, and they can get this paper if they want it, as well as all the other parties to these proceedings, because I have it with me. This is a transcript of a broadcast of B92 Radio of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We have a problem here. Is this going to be tendered into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honour, I can't answer that question at the moment. Your Honour's attempt to get clarification, of course, is most welcome, but given that the amicus prosecutor doesn't have objection to the witness, firstly, clarifying her -- refreshing her memory, and given that this document may well be relevant to Your Honours' determination of this issue, arising, as it does, not from Defence questioning, but from questioning of the Prosecutor, it's my respectful submission that the witness be allowed to answer. And if it appears that the document is relevant, it may well be the case that either the amicus prosecutor or the Defence -- of course, Your Honours suo motu may seek to tender this as an exhibit and have it a part of the record. So, Your Honour, what I would respectfully suggest as a constructive way forward is the witness be allowed to answer, and after that, perhaps, the matter will be clarified, and we make seek to admit the document as part of the court record in some form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: A constructive way for what, sir? It must also be procedural.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't just throw documents into court willy-nilly. There are procedures for tendering evidence into court, and witnesses normally don't come into court with documents. If they are to be refreshed, it is counsel who has the document, who will show that document to the witness, and counsel will say whether he does or does not want to tender the document. Isn't that the procedure?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in domestic systems, of course, it is. And I haven't any idea about the document other than what the witness has kindly mentioned today. But, of course, the strict rules of evidence do not apply. Under Rule 89, of course, all evidence that is relevant may be admitted. And so, Your Honours, if it does emerge, this document may assist in the fair determination of the matter. At that stage it may be that one of the parties may ask Your Honours be seized of it, being professional Judges, not juries. Of course there wouldn't be any prejudice, in my submission. But at this point I can't help further than the observations I've already attempted to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Proceed, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Ms. Kandic, you've --

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say I am a defender of human rights, and on a daily basis I represent victims of war crimes before courts, and I always use documents because I believe it's very important to have my evidence documented and to rely on documents. What I want to say, I can say without any paper, but I wanted to show to you, Honourable Judges, the document itself. And with your leave, it's one sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Answer the lawyer's questions. Don't tell us about how we should run the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Ms. Kandic, you made reference to a single sentence that you wanted to make reference to in your document. Could you read that single sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said the date was 27 February 2007. The reporter of this Radio B92 was interviewing Professor Vojin Dimitrijevic, and she asks him: "Professor, you know that Ms. Kandic said publicly, concerning the judgement, that Serbia had not provided evidence." And he answers: "What Natasa Kandic means are certain transcripts of discussions, deliberations of the supreme body, and they were not presented out of national security concerns, something that the Court always takes into account, but it relates to the issue whether there was intent to exterminate one ethnic community." This is a reference to a redacted portion of the transcript, and what I want to show by this, that this was publicly discussed, even when the question was not asked directly. Here we have Professor Vojin Dimitrijevic who is speaking about this very openly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I'd like to return back to the area that I wanted to question you on, and what I'm interested in knowing is: Prior to the publication of Ms. Hartmann's book, can you tell me what was being debated and by whom?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Human rights organisations, especially in Serbia, discussed this, discussed the fact of the existence of certain documents, military documents, that the public at large will have no access to. This was common knowledge. It was common knowledge that information is concerned in those -- is contained therein not only about the financial support, but other direct support that Serbia provided to Republika Srpska. But not only that. We had a strong doubt that the authorities in Serbia hold the position that the state needs to be protected, regardless of the extent to which Milosevic had turned this state into a criminal one. We used this public opportunity to discuss this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I take it from your answer, then, that when you say it was common knowledge and it was being publicly -- or it was being debated, you're speaking primarily of human rights organisations and people within those organisations that were discussing it and debating it.

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, ordinary people really don't give much thought to this issue, and the public opinion in Serbia still holds the view that national security, regardless of how it is interpreted, needs to be protected. The public in Serbia still does not believe that what the Milosevic regime did was something wrong. I cannot speak about the public opinion because the public opinion still holds that Milosevic was charged wrongly, that he was charged with crimes he had not committed, that the International Criminal Tribunal was established to judge and convict Serbs. That is still the prevailing view in Serbia concerning crimes and responsibility for those crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: So your answer to my question, then, is that the debate and the discussions were primarily within human rights organisations?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We used every opportunity to address this issue publicly. You can find countless news reports and TV broadcasts where I and many other human rights activists discussed this publicly, and of course we always addressed the authorities. We knew very well who was involved in this legal team of Serbia in the case of Bosnia and Herzegovina versus Serbia. We knew the specific people. We knew who was preparing this defence. They frequently wrote in newspapers and scared people that if the judgement should be negative for Serbia, that all future generations, our children, would continue paying reparations for ages, and they even used specific examples, and they would say, Does friends of Jelena Santic -- Jelena Santic being a human rights activist who died a few years ago, but she was taken as an example. They said that her friends would be paying reparations, and those reparations would be received by the friends of Radovan Karadzic. I'm just giving you this example for you to see how publicly this was discussed. Those who were preparing Serbia's legal defence, and they were part of the highest political establishment, spoke about this very publicly and prepared the public to accept anything that the authorities suggest. And in the prevailing atmosphere in Serbia, where the work of the ICTY is not very well accepted, this was very well received. Everybody believed that Serbia had to be defended against charges of genocide and that all means can be used and should be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. That then deals with the question of who was discussing this and debating this. I'd like to turn to the question of what was being discussed and debated in the earlier stages. And my recollection of your previous evidence was that there was some discussion of the SDC minutes and some associated notes. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke about the transcripts of the Supreme Defence Council. We constantly shared our doubts, our suspicions, in fact, that these redacted portions of transcripts contain information about Serbia's involvement and evidence about Serbia's control over and direct cooperation with the police and the army and the authorities of Republika Srpska. And let me add that when the trial started in Serbia, of the members of Skorpions who were charged with liquidation of six Muslim prisoners from Srebrenica, I represented the victims. And as their representative, I had access to all sorts of documents which convinced me even more of the need to continue emphasising in public that all the evidence and all the documents concerning the cooperation between Serbia and Republika Srpska in July and before July 1995 should be public. Those were documents signed at the time by the minister of the police of Republika Srpska, and he had signed papers from which it was obvious that members of the police of the Republic of Serbia were present in the territory of Republika Srpska in July 1995 at the time of the implementation of what the authorities called "Operation Srebrenica," in fact, the liquidation of prisoners. Those documents existed, and people knew that, but nobody spoke about them publicly. I spoke about them publicly. However, the Court, at sentencing stage, accepted the argument of that representative of Republika Srpska who said that he signed these papers showing the presence of the police of the Republic of Serbia in Republika Srpska so that their own fighters would be reassured that they were not alone in liquidating the prisoners, that they were doing that together with people from the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... answer my questions and concentrate on the questions that are being posed. My next question is this: You've made reference to documents that were being discussed and being debated. Did you see any of them?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just speaking of documents that I personally had seen. I have not seen the transcripts of the Supreme Defence Council, themselves. I could not see them if they were in the possession of the highest authorities of the Republic of Serbia, the military authorities. Nobody had access to them, but they were seen by the Judges of the ICTY. I have never seen them, although I would like to. And as I said, I believe it is important for the entire public to see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: You've already indicated, then, that you were speaking publicly about them. You've now indicated that you hadn't seen them. So what you were relating to other people was your best understanding or some speculation as to the nature of the documents and what was in the documents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Needless to say, I, as well as other champions of human rights, had not seen those documents, but a while ago I quoted to you what Professor Vojin Dimitrijevic said, and I believe that he has seen those documents because he participated in the preparation of Serbia's defence. Let me reiterate. He says what were our public doubts. He says Natasa Kandic is referring to the SDC's transcripts, and she believes that those transcripts are hiding evidence about the intentions of Serbia to commit -- to participate in the commission of genocide, simply speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Kandic, you've just indicated that members of the human rights organisations and the champions in this area had not seen the documents, but were similarly speaking out, so what we have are a number of people speaking out who are speculating as to what is in the documents; is that not accurate?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wonder whether you understand what I'm saying. Of course, nobody ever said that we were talking about the transcripts of the Supreme Defence Council on the basis of our own access to those documents. You are suggesting that perhaps I and others are speaking on the basis of someone having granted us access to those documents. No, those documents were not public, and we were aware of the fact that those documents were not public. I knew that it was important for those documents to be made public, and that is why I always -- whenever I appear in the media, I always said how important it was for the Serbian authorities to disclose those documents. When I took the stand last time, I mentioned that at a roundtable gathering in connection with the judgment of International Court of Justice of the 29th of June, 2007, Professor Rade Stojanovic, the leader of the defence team of Serbia, also said at a certain point the time that he thought that the seal should be lifted from those documents, that they should be made public, that those documents should be disclosed. He, himself, said so. But specifically to answer your question, of course, I always spoke on the basis of what was very symptomatic. Documents were hidden. Why would the Republic of Serbia hide documents? Why wouldn't it grant access to them? First of all, because, on the one hand, Milosevic, and later the new authorities, accepted Milosevic's position and Milosevic's explanation to the effect that Serbia was never at war. Why were the new authorities be hiding documents about the cooperation between the Republic of Serbia and the Republika Srpska if they do not contain evidence which can actually bring to light some new facts about that cooperation, pertinent to the indictment -- to the charges of the ICTY against Milosevic or against some other people charged with genocide, for the genocide committed in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Kandic. I'd like to return back to my question to you, and that has to do with the nature of the discussions that we're going on, the nature of the debate. From what you've said, it seems to me that what we're talking about is people making comments based on assumptions and speculation. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We constantly advanced a request for the redacted portions of military documents to be disclosed, that that was important for Serbia, that it was important for relations between Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that it was important for the creation of some sort of a normal democratic future in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. We thought that to be the most important and that every state -- in this particular case, Serbia had the obligation to the victims and to its own society, the obligation being to disclose all facts having to do with Serbia's responsibility for the committed wrongdoings in this concrete case for the genocide committed in Srebrenica. That was not our comment; in other words, it was my request and the request advanced by other human rights organisations, as well as by numerous jurists, and actually not those who were part of the authorities, for the secret documents to be disclosed, primarily the transcripts of the Supreme Defence Council, but also other documents in respect of which the Republic of Serbia also requested the granting of protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. MacFarlane, please control your witness. That long speech doesn't answer your question --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Perhaps my initial question might shed some light on this. Ms. Kandic, in some of the original documents filed in these proceedings, you were described as a high-profile militant for human rights. My question to you is: Do you agree with that characterisation of you, and if so, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, I think this is an inappropriate question, for you to ask me whether I believe that I'm a high-profile militant. Please put that question to some other people, not to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: You are declining to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that it is courteous. That is as if somebody asks you at this moment, Do you believe yourself to be a good amicus prosecution at this moment? It is just not a decent question. There's always other people that one asks about their opinions of other people, especially about some public activists or human rights champions, or you should ask the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you, and my question is this: That, Ms. Hartmann, through her counsel, has suggested that you're a high-profile militant. And my question is: Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, in fact, don't know what "militant" exactly means. I'm very committed to facts, the truth, and justice. And whatever I do, I do in a very dedicated way, by spending three weeks, a month, in court representing -- the fact that I do that, that I represent victims for three weeks per month in court, speaks something about my commitment and my dedication, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Maybe I can suggest this to you, then, to see if you agree with this or not. You have been characterized by Ms. Hartmann, through her counsel, as a high-profile militant. Does that then mean that in coming to testify, you want to make sure that your message is conveyed, regardless of the questions that are being posed to you?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I fail to comprehend your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I'm suggesting to you that in coming to these proceedings, your main objective is to bring a message, and you want to convey that message to the Chamber almost regardless of what --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, we object to that question. And I apologise for interrupting my colleague. But before he can put such a proposition to the witness, Your Honour, he has to establish a foundation, a basis for that proposition. The qualification that was given of Ms. Kandic was, as the Prosecutor pointed out quite rightly, that of counsel, not that of Ms. Kandic, so he can put questions. But I think putting such a suggestion without any foundation for it is, in our view, inappropriate, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: If I might respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Foundation has been laid, in my respectful submission. Two points. Number 1, the characterisation comes from my learned friend directly and from the accused, through counsel. Number 2, we have heard a number of speeches this morning. And I'm endeavouring to determine if those speeches, which were non-responsive to my questions, were simply messages that are being delivered to this Chamber by a militant human rights activist. That is the objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if we may, we believe of the Chamber, we'll just add one thing. If the Prosecutor were putting his questions more precisely and not in the broad, general, and non-precise way which he has, I believe that Ms. Kandic would be able to answer the questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Objection overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Let me go back to my question, then, Ms. Kandic. I'm suggesting to you that you are a militant human rights activist and your main objective today is to convey a message to the Chamber and to the Tribunal and to the world. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the way I see my role is that I am to say -- present what I've been saying over the past years in connection with the case in which Florence Hartmann is charged. I am only speaking and adducing facts about what I've been saying in the past few years and about what other human rights activists have been saying, and also how the Defence team of Serbia reacted and what it was that they said about the redacted portions of the transcript of the military Supreme Defence Council. And just like I have been saying throughout these years, I repeat today, I always consider that the redacted portions of the transcript should be disclosed and made accessible to the public, and that is all. In earlier years and today, that is all that I am saying. And of course my question in that connection is the following: Why is Florence Hartmann on trial if I and scores of other human rights activists, jurists, experts on international humanitarian law, experts on freedom of expression, and great champions of the spreading of international justice have been demanding for years for those documents to be made public, and for Serbia and no other state of the former Yugoslavia, for that matter, to be able to invoke Article 54 of the Rules of Procedure of the ICTY and to hide away important documents from the eyes of the public?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Kandic. I believe that you've essentially answered my question. Almost regardless of what I pose to you, you'll be giving a speech. My question to you is whether or not --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, we object to that sort of comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: The record will be clear on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, the record can be made in final submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, sir. If you do object, please give a basis for your objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we object to Mr. MacFarlane making comments about the evidence that is being given. If he were to ask his question in a precise way, and if he wants to make anything he wishes at the end of the case of the evidence that is given, the proper form for that, Your Honour, in our submission, is the final brief and the final arguments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: That submission has already been made, and the Chamber has ruled on it. I endeavour to pose specific questions to the witness, and so far all I've received are speeches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I would like to move on to the next area to see if we can make progress, and that is with respect to the discussion -- the public discussion that you talked about concerning not the minutes and not the notes and associated documents, but purported decisions of this Chamber or this Tribunal. So my focused question is with respect to the discussions and the debates concerning the decisions, as opposed to the documents, and my question to you is: Had you seen and have you seen any of these purported decisions?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally had not seen those decisions, but there was talk in the public about those decisions. And, namely, what was said was the Court had decided -- they used the term "decision," but just as when I read this sentence uttered by Professor Vojin Dimitrijevic, he said it was the Court that had decided that those documents or the portions of those documents should be secret, so the Court -- the Tribunal was referred to. The Court decided it was something that belonged to the Court. There was no specific talk about the decision adopted in 2003 or in some other year. It was not referred to in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Based on the discussions that were going on concerning these decisions, what was your understanding on the number of decisions? Are we speaking of one, or two, or three, or five? How many decisions are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood that two decisions were in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: How many people would you say you've spoken to about these decisions?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that we discussed most the redacted portions, and about the content and our suspicions as to what was the content of those documents, and we also spoke how we could not understand why a decision to the effect that those documents should be declared secret should have been adopted. That is what was the gist of our discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the decisions, the speculation was that there was two decisions. What further information came --

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was reference to the existence of these decisions, but it didn't matter to me and to the others how many of the decisions there were. What mattered was that by those decisions, some important documents have been hidden from the public. It turned out that also in the case of the International Court of Justice, those documents were not accessible either, and we thought - I am referring to myself and to other human rights activists - thought that it was not good, that it was bad, that this was not a proper relationship towards the past, that this was not a proper relationship -- attitude towards victims. And we thought that we were bound by the principles of Louis Joinet and Diane Orentlicher, some experts, in other words, who in their line of duty dealt with some very important issues which concern also the right of individuals, of victims, and of societies to know, including their right to be familiar with the evidence which is actually hidden by the redacted portions of the transcript of the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... narrow one, and a very simple one. I'd be grateful --

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one intervention that may assist my learned friend. I do note that after he asks the question in English, he takes his headphone off when the witness is answering, and I think this is the reason why on a few occasions there has been an overlap between the translation of the answer and then my friend's subsequent question. So perhaps if there can be a pause, it would help, because we've missed some translation of the answer that was being given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for that intervention, Mr. Khan. If you could -- I'm talking to both witness and counsel. If you could pause between question and answer so that we give the translators an opportunity to finish their translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Ms. Kandic, my question is a very focused and a simple one, and I would be grateful if you could answer that question. The question is this: How many people did you speak to about the decisions?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is clear from all my answers that I cannot give you a specific number of persons. Sometimes I spoke about it in some written text, in an interview, the consequence of that being that many people read about it. Those people who read about it talked about it with other people. So when the public airing of comments and views is in question, it is hard to tell what the number of persons with whom I spoke was. Perhaps with 50 people, either human rights champions or experts -- international, regional, national experts. Perhaps I talked with them about our suspicions as to what could be contained in these documents of the military defence council. We talked so as to devise a way in which we could bring pressure to bear for those documents to be disclosed. But I repeat, I spoke about it publicly, I also spoke about it publicly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. MacFarlane, we've got to finish. Please control your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I'll pose one further question in this area, Ms. Kandic, and I would urge you to provide me with an answer which is responsive to my question. My question is this: I'm suggesting to you that a large number of people were discussing these decisions, virtually none of whom had actually seen the decisions, so what we're talking about is a series of assumptions and speculation as to these decisions. Is that a fair assessment of what was going on?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I and the other human rights activists talked about what those decisions had done. By those decisions were hidden from the public important documents. That is what was the subject of our talks. Mind you, the fact that it was a decision is the form -- that is what formally actually led to the substance. The substance was that there existed secret documents. We wanted a secret document disclosed. That was the essence of our public demand, for the disclosure of those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Kandic, you have just told us that there were references to the existence of the decisions. Would you be kind enough to provide more explanation as to the contents of the references? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The way I understood it was that the Judges had handed down decisions on the basis of which Serbia's request was accepted to the effect that certain parts of the transcript of the military Supreme Defence Council should be confidential, should be secret; namely, documents that we doubted -- that we suspected were pertinent to the period when the genocide in Srebrenica was committed. That's what we talked about. We did not talk about nor was our request focused on the decisions, themselves. All we asked for was for those documents which became confidential by virtue of some decisions, for those documents to be disclosed. That's was what was important for us, for those documents to become public and for the public to gain access to the redacted parts of the transcript. We always talked about the content of the document, what was behind the redacted parts of the document. That was what we were talking about, that was what mattered to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Kandic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to another issue, and that is the conference that you assisted in organising in Belgrade, and you talked about that on your last occasion here, which was held on the 29th of June of 2007. Do you recall that discussion?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Which roundtable -- which talk? There's nothing associated with the 12th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Twenty-nine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. The 29th, I'm told it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I apologise, it is the 29th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Let me read the heading of the document that was discussed last week -- on the last occasion to see if that assists. It is "Humanitarian Law Centre in Belgrade, 29 June 2007, Regional Debate on the Judgement of the International Court of Justice on Genocide." Do you recall that discussion?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Of course, I recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I'd like you to give us a sense of the format of that conference, and in particular the discussion on the minutes and the notes that we've been talking about. Was it a panel discussion? Was it a large group discussion? Was it individual presentations? Can you give us a sense and a flavour of the format.

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a roundtable discussion with participants from the Defence team of Serbia and from the Defence team of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Then other participants were jurists from all the states of the former Yugoslavia, as well as human rights activists and champions from the entire region. This was a regional specialist gathering. There were about 40 participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: And it's my understanding that a number of people spoke to the question of protected documents and decisions, and they were expressing their own views on that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was very much on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: There were being different views that were being expressed. On occasion, one or more of the participants noted the need for care in discussing these matters because they were confidential; is that not accurate?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall anything of the kind having been said by anyone. I do believe that Sasa Obradovic did, but it wasn't important because all the other participants, including the Serbian Defence team leader, Radoslav Stojanovic, were in favour of those documents being disclosed, so that we actually again discussed the essence -- the content of those documents. He said that he would very much like to have those transcripts disclosed because then it would be seen that they contained nothing important, that there was no important evidence in them at all. And I expected that something would really happen, because if someone who was the leader of the Defence team of the Republic of Serbia was publicly advocating the disclosure of the transcripts at such a gathering, that that would indeed happen, and I supported his position strongly that they be disclosed, because when he said that it will then be seen that there is nothing in them to the effect of what was being publicly said, I said, Of course, then do disclose them. Let us have access to those documents to see what it is that they are hiding from the public, what is hidden in those documents. What impressed me most was about Professor Rade Stojanovic, just like myself and other human rights activists, and he was the Defence team leader, demanded the opening, the disclosure of these confidential and redacted portions of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we proceed, I wanted to give a chance to the witness to give her answer to the question, but we object to the manner and the unfairness, in our submission, in which the question is posed to the witness. The amicus asked whether a participant, or participants, he said, noted the need for care in discussing this matter because they were confidential. In our submission, Your Honour, and we will readdress the matter in re-examination, if Mr. MacFarlane wishes to put to the witness that a participant or several participants gave a warning to that effect, he should specify what the warning pertained to. As I mentioned, Your Honour, we will address that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He just said it pertained to the confidentiality of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, the problem, Your Honour, is it doesn't. The transcript will reveal what it refers to, and we'll deal to that in a moment. But Mr. MacFarlane should be careful, when he puts the question, to specify that it was, in fact, the content of the SDC minutes that were referred to by the parties in question, not the decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux, if you prefer to advise Mr. MacFarlane how to put his questions, maybe you can do that later. I just am not going to interfere in Mr. MacFarlane's manner of asking questions, unless what he does is irregular in terms of the Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, obviously this is the Chamber's ruling, and I'm not trying to interfere with it, but if Mr. MacFarlane wishes to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then if you accept that it is the Chamber's ruling, then unless you disagree with it and you want to take it on appeal, you can take it on appeal, you don't have to comment on it any further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Ms. Kandic, you indicated that you weren't sure if anyone had expressed concerns about being careful concerning confidential documents or confidential decisions. Let me see if I can refresh your memory on this. At page 93 and 94 of the book that you had on the last occasion, the following is attributed to Sasa Obradovic as follows: "I shan't go into this issue here, but it's as simple as that if you come by a document which has been protected from public eye by The Hague Tribunal, then you are committing an offence of disrespecting the Tribunal. You know, some journalists from Croatia have answered for something like this." Do you recall hearing that during the discussion, and do you recall seeing that in your book?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me remind you, I did say a moment ago that Sasa Obradovic said something like that, but that was a completely minor comment relative to countless other speeches and comments concerning the redacted portions of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Are you saying that it was a minor comment, that someone with the Serbian Embassy was cautioning people about the prospects of committing an offence and the need for care? That was a minor comment, in your view?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sasa Obradovic was an employee of the embassy, and next to him stood Professor Stojanovic, who had led Serbia's Defence team. And he was saying that he was in favour of those documents that had been proclaimed confidential by the Judges of the ICTY being made public. And in my eyes, it was much more important, what Professor Stojanovic was saying, than a simple employee, Sasa Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Is it not true that that simple employee, Sasa Obradovic, was also a lawyer employed with the embassy?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know who and what Sasa Obradovic is. Embassies have large staffs. And as far as I understood, he was helping the Defence team, but he had no high-profile role. Professor Stojanovic was very well known, on the contrary. He was a professor at our university's law school, he was a prominent participant of that roundtable panel of 29th June 2007, and he said very clearly that the objective of Serbia's legal team was to defend Serbia from charges of genocide and that the legal team succeeded in that. Now, the effect of that was that I and the others asked questions later. Did they succeed because certain documents were not accessible; namely, the transcripts of the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Ms. Kandic, my questions at this point focus entirely on the role that Sasa Obradovic played at this conference. You indicated that, in your view, his comment, which was a cautionary one, was a minor comment, but later on in that same excerpt that you have in your book, that same individual, Mr. Obradovic, said this: "I'm talking here exclusively as a lawyer, and I was invited here as one, as the representative of Serbia and Montenegro before the ICJ." Is that not true? Do you not recall that?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only repeat what I said earlier. We invited Professor Stojanovic, and I know we had invited Vladimir Djeric because he was well known to the public. Before 2004, he was a very good lawyer, employed by the foreign ministry, and the public knew him very well as someone who was dealing with issues connected with the case of Bosnia and Herzegovina versus Serbia, whereas Sasa Obradovic was not a public figure. It was probably Professor Stojanovic who had suggested that he take part in the panel. I don't think we invited Sasa Obradovic, ourselves. He might have been a member of the team or perhaps a technical assistant to the team, but he was a civil servant, a civil servant whose job it was to defend the positions, the demands, and the decisions of his state. I don't think anything is controversial here. I can just say what I said before, that at that meeting Sasa Obradovic's role was to defend. When I said that there is a lot of evidence that members of the Serbian police and army had taken part in the slaughter of Srebrenica, he said, yes, but there exists such a thing as the Nicaragua test.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I want to be clear, then, on what you're saying to the Chamber. You're saying that Mr. Obradovic intervened, his comment was a minor one, in your opinion it was insignificant because he was a civil servant, even though he was employed as a lawyer at the Serbian Embassy and had appeared before the ICJ on behalf of Serbia? Is that what you're saying to this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me be even more specific. In my eyes, he was a civil servant who had orders, instructions, to read the transcript, see what's bad for Serbia in there, because the trial of Serbia before the ICJ is coming. I believe that he and other lawyers in various state agencies were instructed to read these documents and see what would be a bad thing to be seen by the International Criminal Tribunal and the ICJ, be it in the case before the ICJ or indictments by the ICTY. There's no dispute about this. Sasa Obradovic did not dominate over this round-panel discussion. What was dominant was the discussion whether this judgement by the ICJ had brought justice, and some participants, including me, said that the judgement did not bring justice, primarily because it did not have access to documents that we believed contained evidence about Serbia's involvement in Srebrenica. And I also quoted many other documents from which it is obvious that Serbia even participated in the liquidation of prisoners in Srebrenica, and Sasa Obradovic responded to that by saying that we should take into account the Nicaragua test and what the Judges of the ICJ had decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Ms. Kandic --

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first you ask me a question, and then you don't want to hear the answer. You ask me one thing, and when I tell you what was relevant about Sasa Obradovic's arguments, you don't want to hear it. Yes, the Nicaragua test was his argument, countering my arguments and those of other participants that there is concrete evidence about the cooperation between the Republic of Serbia and Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Ms. Kandic, in these proceedings it's very important for you to listen to the question that I pose and be responsive to that question. I'm not asking for speeches. I don't think there is any point in proceeding further on that particular point. What I'd like to now move to is some recent speeches which have been provided by the Prosecutor in this Tribunal and by the President of this Tribunal, and I'm going to be focusing on the question of the cooperation of states.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that the -- I'm going to ask that the two statements that I'll be drawing to the attention of the witness be distributed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters would also appreciate a copy of the two relevant statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. MacFarlane, do you have sufficient copies for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Just to caution my learned friend that their microphone is on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Ms. Kandic, I'd like you to look, first of all, at the document headed "Statement" on the front page, and address of Serge Brammertz, and I will read the relevant parts to you so that you can understand it in your preferred language. But for everyone else in the proceedings, I'll be describing the nature of the document and then proceeding to page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. MacFarlane, without wanting to interfere, we are going to be going for a break in a minute's time. Do you think you want to start this new topic now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: No, I think it would be best after the break. It's a whole new area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Shall we then take the break at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: That's fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I did take the opportunity during the break to review my notes, and I'm pleased to say that I've been able to reduce the areas that I intend to pursue, and my best estimate is that the balance of my cross-examination will be in the vicinity of half an hour, maybe a little bit more, but in that range.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Ms. Kandic, do you have the document headed "Statement Address of Serge Brammertz..." before you?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: And just so that the record is complete, I'm referring to a document which has been marked as tab 2 for these proceedings, headed "Statement Address of Serge Brammertz, Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia to the Security Council for June 2009," directed to Mr. President, Mr. Prime Minister, Excellencies, and it's dated at the top, the 4th of June, 2009. This is then a statement to the Security Council just a matter of three or three and a half weeks ago. And I am asking you to turn to page 2, and I will read it to you so that you can consider it in your language. I'm going to direct your attention only to the first two paragraphs, actually, after the little stars at the top, the two paragraphs immediately after that. And the first one reads as follows: "The cooperation of states with my office remains critical to the successful completion of our trials and appeals work." Do you see that, and did you hear me read that into the record?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: The Prosecutor was, therefore, emphasising that the cooperation of states was important to the work of the OTP. You see that emphasis in that statement?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Do you agree with the Prosecutor when he says that?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Moving to the second paragraph, it reads as follows: "We continue to request the assistance from Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, and Serbia in a number of areas, such as the provision of documents, access to archives, ensuring that witnesses can testify before the Tribunal, and assisting in locating and arresting fugitives." Do you see that portion of it, and did you hear me read it into the record in your language?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it, I heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Do you agree with that statement as well?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I take it that on the basis of those two statements, that you do recognise that state cooperation with the Tribunal is very important.

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Important to bring offenders to justice, and it's important to ensure that witnesses are treated properly, and victims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: My question to you is this: Given the importance of the cooperation of states -- sorry. Before I get to that question, before I get to the question: Are you familiar with the concept of protective measures, particularly as regards victims?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the concept of protective measures on the application of a state?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes; not in detail, not in every detail, but I know that under the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the ICTY, states are entitled to seek protective measures when national security is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you. My question to you is this, Ms. Kandic: Would it surprise you if, in the event of routine breaches of protective measures sought and received by states, that a state might start to reconsider its cooperation with the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this question of yours is really speculative. I don't know of any example of a state seeking a reconsideration of protective measures. At no time did Serbia threaten -- for instance, after that statement of Professor Rade Stojanovic that he believed the transcripts of the SDC should be disclosed, no one from the Serbian authorities said that, In that case, we would no longer provide documents under protective measures, because these were states, parties to the conflict, and they must not blackmail the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Let me put my question slightly differently, and I'd like to get your reaction to it. I suggest to you that it is important to enforce protective measures sought by a state and received by a state in order to ensure their continuing cooperation with the Tribunal, including, for instance, Serbia.

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my opinion, that is shared by many experts in freedom of expression and experts for justice following armed conflicts, that protective measures must not prejudice justice. Protective measures for witnesses are extremely important, but it has turned out that the Tribunal imposes protective measures here while witnesses testify, but these measures and protection do not continue after the witnesses return to their home country. I repeat, protective measures must correspond to the need for courts to establish facts, and, in criminal trials, to establish the responsibility of the accused, and, when we speak about the ICJ, to establish state responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Let's move in a little bit more closely, then, to the point. I take it from what you've said so far that you do support protective measures in connection with witnesses and victims.

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I support them, because there are witnesses who are in danger, and unless they are relocated, their life would be in danger, because if they talk about crimes in which members of the police and the army of their home country were involved, then their life would be in danger in that country. Therefore, I strongly support very precise and very broad protective measures for such witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Turning now to the question of protective measures for states, do you similarly support the ability of states to seek protective measures and have them evaluated by the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will stick with the example of the former Yugoslavia. What is in issue there was a war that did not -- that was not contained in the territory of one state. It took place in the territories of a number of states, excepting Serbia and Montenegro. But if there are war crimes trials arising from that conflict, and if proceedings are held before the ICJ to establish the responsibility of individual states for such crimes, then if there is evidence, relevant evidence that one state claims involves its national security interests, then the Court has to balance these requests for protective measures with a need to administer justice. If a large number of such evidence and documents are not accessible, then it might happen that the Court fails to administer justice in such a way as to guarantee that such conflicts would not be repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Ms. Kandic, where a state has sought and obtained protective measures, do you support its enforcement in the event of a breach?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, as a champion of human rights, in this case and before - I don't know exactly when these decisions were adopted - always advocated that there should be no confidential documents when war crimes trials arising from crimes in the former Yugoslavia were concerned. I always advocated that all documents concerning crimes in the states of the former Yugoslavia should be public, that it's important to establish facts in a public way, so that we are able to see what Milosevic and his regime exactly did when they brought our people and our country into a situation when they are under sanctions, when they were later accused of involvement in genocide, and the whole country was accused of involvement in numerous crimes that led to the death of thousands and thousands. Independently of that, I always advocated that there should be no confidential documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Are you then saying that you do not have confidence in the ability of this Tribunal to properly analyse an application and do the balancing that's required on the application of a state for protective measures?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I should like to say that I am a champion of human rights, and my basic task is to advocate what are the principles on which respect for fundamental human rights are based and the rights of societies to the truth, the right to have facts established on the basis of which the accountability of either individuals or states shall be established. Along those lines, I always and on every occasion have to work for the families of the victims and for society to be made available facts and for all facts to be publicly disclosed, facts which can help establish why things happened and why war crimes happened. That is the only way in which we can come up with guarantees for the kind of crime that has happened to be never repeated. This is something that I have learned. I learned this from the top experts on transitional justice. This is something I read while reading Joinet, Bassiouni, or Orentlicher. Apart from that, I also appreciate the fact that both the Prosecution's and Tribunal's courts have to ensure sufficient guarantees, after international trials, that there will be no repetition of crimes. But if documents are hidden, there will never be peace. They will always keep saying that Serbia's hiding some documents, that we do not know the exact truth. On the other hand, we have countless individuals saying that they know that through its police and army, Serbia directly participated in the commission of genocide in Srebrenica. I've talked to many people who would never say so publicly, who are afraid to do so, but it is, in a way, common knowledge; namely, irrespective of these decisions on confidential documents and the hiding of these documents, it is necessary for the truth to be known, but for the truth to be known, it has to be publicly recognised as such. If documents are hidden, the truth will never be publicly demonstrated, publicised, and therefore it will be never recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Ms. Kandic, I have one question left on this particular point. It's a focused question. I would ask you to simply indicate whether you agree or disagree with me. And the question is this: You seem to be saying that you agree with the concept of protective measures for victims and support that, but that you don't have the same sort of support for protective measures at the instance of a state. Is that accurate or not?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not accurate. It stems from what I have said, that I do not agree for protective measures, vis-a-vis states, participants in armed conflicts in respect of which there are serious indications that they might be accountable for the commission of the gravest crimes, including genocide; namely, states, participants in armed conflicts, are excluded by me from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: So certain types of protective measures at the instance of a state you would support, others you would not; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying and what is extremely important for me is that there should be no confidential documents where states, participants in armed conflicts, are concerned. I never referred to protective measures in respect of states that have nothing to do with either war crimes or armed conflicts, armed conflicts which are the subject of trials. And I'm not quite certain that I can competently give you the rationale for that at this point in time. I would require some time to read through a lot of material in order to come up with a meritorious position. What I'm referring to, in regard of this position, is that it refers to states which are not directly associated with an armed conflict. They have some documents that can be of assistance to shed light on facts, but they have some reasons that they are guided by because of their national security concerns. But when we are talking about states, participants in armed conflicts, my position is quite clear on that score. I'm against their invoking of their vital national interest and national security being actually accepted if, in that way, they hide some documents. I proceed from the fact that after armed conflicts are finished, like was the case in Serbia, the new authorities must not continue the policy of defending Serbia in the same way as Milosevic and his institutions, institutions under his control, did. They absolutely must adopt a different approach, and that means that they have to adduce all facts which will shed light on what that state -- what that system did and the way in which it contributed, i.e., participated in the commission of the gravest crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: The final question in this area, Ms. Kandic is: So that, in essence, what you're saying is that Serbia, Bosnia, and Croatia have no right to ask for protective measures; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that a state charged with the gravest crimes, such as genocide, as Serbia was charged, should not have the right -- does not have the right to hide important documents, any documents, because no invoking of national security interest can make up for -- substitute the need to establish the truth, the facts. Representatives of Serbia and authorities have publicly explained why defence by all available means is important. They sought to frighten the citizens of Serbia, saying that each one of them will have to pay reparations. But I feel once the authorities changed, as was the case in Serbia, the new authorities should not do that; that they should be committed to the need to establish facts; that they should adopt the proper attitude to the crimes that were committed and to the role of its institutions in those events. What I mean is that a so-charged state should not be allowed to maintain documents confidential, because in that case it actually is keeping secret documents which actually give the right to the victims and to all injured parties to suspect that it is precisely that state that is accountable, that the state is indeed accountable for what it is being charged with, for the genocide that it is being charged with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Ms. Kandic, I'd like to move on to a new area. This will be the second-last area I'd like to talk to you about. It's completely different from what we've been talking about in the past. This has to do with the decision-making process within the Humanitarian Law Centre. You mentioned earlier that there is a board of management within the centre?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: And Ms. Hartmann, amongst others, is on that board?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: How many persons, in total, are a part of the board of management of the centre?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: In terms of the decision-making process within the centre, would it be accurate to say that on key issues, on key positions, that there is a consensus-building, there is a collective decision-making process, as opposed to simply one person making the decision? Would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a consensus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Over the years, you have had occasion to deal with governments in different parts of this area of the world?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, but our contacts with governments were mainly linked to war crimes trials and the need to establish facts. We do not have any political context with governments because we are not a political party. Our context exclusively have to do with our basic activity, which is the establishment of justice following armed conflicts, and it is pursuant to that that we maintain our contacts with the governments in the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that governments, being a large organisation, and indeed any large organisation, have the same sort of decision-making process, that is, a collective decision-making process, similar to your centre?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, frankly, do not know how governments are organized, and I do not have that many contacts with governments in the region. We exclusively established such contacts when there is a pronounced need for us to help in war crimes trials. For instance, in the year 2004, the Ministry of Justice of the Republic of Croatia was gotten in touch with in connection with war crimes trials in Belgrade because the trials started with the massive case of the liquidation of Croatian prisoners, so I addressed the Ministry of Justice of the Republic of Croatia, requesting them to assist us in encouraging the witnesses, the injured parties, to come and testify. This is the extent of my liaising with governments, apart from the fact that as a citizen, I follow the speed with which the process of the democratic-building of society is evolving or is inhibited. Otherwise, I have no reason to seek any additional contact or explanations from government or to familiarise myself with the way in which they adopt their decisions. I follow the work of parliaments and the way in which they adopt their decisions, the agenda of the parliaments in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia, but as a citizen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slow down. The interpreter is struggling to keep pace with you, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Ms. Kandic, I want to move into the last area of my questions, and this has to do with your connection with Ms. Hartmann, the accused in these proceedings. At the beginning of your testimony, you outlined the nature of the relationship and your contact with her going back a number of years. When was the last time you spoke to Ms. Hartmann?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of May this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: You indicated that you were sorry to see her charged?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the sense that I was sorry in that way. I thought that it was unjust, and I've been saying for years -- I've been protesting against this and the way in which the disclosure of these documents was prevented. And not only I, myself, but many other people, too. And it seemed unjust to me that she should be charged with this, and I was there actually advocating the disclosure of these documents, not speaking about myself only. There are countless other human rights champions, journalists, jurists. Also the president of the board of management of the Humanitarian Law Centre is a renowned jurist, Professor Pajic. He, too, has been advocating this, and many other jurists, international jurists, those dealing with international law, namely. They all have been strongly raising their voices in favour of the fact that the transparency of court trials should actually rule out decisions which will declare confidential many important pieces of evidence and declare them confidential documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: I'm not speaking now of other persons, and I'm not speaking of documents, but I'm rather focusing on how you feel about these proceedings. And my suggestion to you, and I want to get your reaction, is that you think that it was unfair for Ms. Hartmann to be charged.

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not about feelings, you know. This is my principled attitude. It is not that I am sorry for her, irrespective of what she's been charged with, that I feel sorry for her and that that is why I've been saying what I've been saying for years. This is not about that. This is not about friendship, about emotions. This is about a highly-important professional issue, and that is my position, vis-a-vis that issue, regardless of whether Florence Hartmann is in question or somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: My final question is this: I take it, from what you've said, that you would not want to see the accused convicted.

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I again have to correct that expression of yours. You say that I would not want to see her convicted. I profoundly believe that there is not a single real reason - I'm referring to the realm of truth and justice - for her to be convicted. In my view, this trial should serve to reconsider -- re-examine the decision -- the adoption of a decision for those transcripts to be at long last disclosed so that we might eliminate all these doubts, dispel all these suspicions, in terms of the evidence about the crimes in Srebrenica and all the other things which happened in 1992 and 1993. For us, the citizens of the countries of the states formed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, it is very important to actually be confronted with that past. Now, the fact that we do not have the best of authorities, the democratic authorities that we need to have, that is why, inter alia, this issue is so important. We need to stop supporting something which still belongs to the old authorities, which is the ownership of Milosevic's regime. I believe it is very important for us not to have any secret in respect of that state, in respect of Milosevic, that we stop creating myths and compel today's authorities to act in accordance with facts, no matter how embarrassing, how difficult, those facts might be. But what Milosevic's state did is something that we need to know the truth about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Ms. Kandic, based on what you've said, I suggest that you perceive these proceedings as a vehicle to achieve your agenda and your objective, and that is the disclosure of the documents. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I avail myself of every opportunity to say that we should not have secrets, that we should exert pressure on the authorities for them to renounce that tool of theirs, that of manipulating and of hiding. We need guarantees that there will be no more crimes, and one of such guarantees is that what has been declared a secret should be disclosed. Now, the fact that you are interpreting this in this way, namely, you keep accusing me that I'm some sort of an orator, a politician, that I'm using this for promoting my personal objectives, I have no personal objectives. All my objectives are based on what I have learned since the beginning of this war, which is that the truth and facts are the most important of all. Please, I have no private objectives. I have no power. I am just a mere human rights activist who has learned, after all these years -- who has come to understand the facts. The disclosure of facts can be of the greatest assistance to us. I live there. You don't live there. I want our future to be brighter. I want us to force these authorities to make available to us all facts concerning the past. I want them to tell us the facts, to tell us where the graves are, mass graves are, to show us the transcripts of this army. The army is not innocent at all. The generals are at large, and thousands of people have been killed. I want us to actually lift the veil of mystery from the police and from the army and to give priority to what is professional, and nothing is professional if documents are hidden behind it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, ma'am. You have not been asked a question. The Prosecutor said he has finished. Mr. Mettraux, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. And perhaps before we start, we have a bundle of document for the witness, the Chamber, and the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Kandic. Do you recall being asked a number of questions by the Prosecutor, both two weeks ago, when you first came, and earlier this morning, about a comment, or I think it was called a warning, that Sasa Obradovic gave to Ms. Hadzovic? Do you remember those questions?

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can I ask you to turn to what is tab number 1 of the series of document that I've given to you. You will see, sir, a number of it's extracts from the transcript of the 29th of June, 2007, conference in Belgrade that you helped organise, and I ask you, if you may, to turn to page 40, 4-0, please. Can you see here, at the --

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot. Page 40, you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: NATASA KANDIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
